front: Under the FDA scheme, what are the three medical device classes and their controls?
back: Class I: General Controls. Class II: General + Special Controls. Class III: General Controls + Premarket Approval.

front: Which FDA device class carries the lowest risk, and which the greatest?
back: Class I is lowest risk; Class III is greatest risk.

front: Which FDA requirements apply to every medical device class?
back: General Controls — the baseline FD&C Act requirements apply to Class I, II and III.

front: For a non-exempt Class I or II device, what premarket submission is generally required?
back: A 510(k) premarket notification.

front: What two things does FDA device classification depend on (besides risk)?
back: The device's intended use and its indications for use.

front: When did FDA's Quality Management System Regulation (QMSR) take effect?
back: February 2, 2026 (amending 21 CFR Part 820 device CGMP).

front: Which international standard does the FDA QMSR incorporate by reference?
back: ISO 13485:2016 — Medical devices, quality management systems.

front: Who must supply the technician with specific written directions for each case?
back: The dentist, via the prescription; the dentist must also be available to answer the technician's questions.

front: How closely must a technician follow the dentist's prescription?
back: Exactly.

front: How should a technician treat what they learn about a patient's dental condition or personal life?
back: As privileged information — not repeated outside professional conversation.

front: To whom does the AFPAM say the technician's moral responsibility lies?
back: The patient.

front: Under OSHA's BBP standard, how often must the written exposure control plan be updated?
back: At least annually (also documenting consideration of safer devices and frontline worker input).

source.ref: OSHA Fact Sheet: Bloodborne Pathogens Standard (29 CFR 1910.1030)

front: Which OSHA standard is the Bloodborne Pathogens standard (CFR citation)?

source.ref: OSHA Fact Sheet: Bloodborne Pathogens Standard (29 CFR 1910.1030)

front: What is the origin and insertion of the masseter?
back: Origin: zygomatic arch. Insertion: lateral surface of the mandibular ramus.

front: Primary action of the masseter?
back: Elevates (closes) the mandible; may aid protrusion.

front: Where does the temporalis insert?
back: On the coronoid process of the mandible.

front: Besides closing the jaw, what important movement does the temporalis produce?
back: Retrusion — pulling the mandible back.

front: Where does the medial pterygoid insert?
back: Medial (internal) surface of the mandibular ramus.

front: Where does the lateral pterygoid insert?
back: Neck of the condyloid process of the mandible.

front: What happens when both lateral pterygoids contract together?
back: The mandible is pulled forward into protrusion (opening slightly).

front: What do the paired mylohyoid muscles form?
back: The floor of the mouth (attached to the mylohyoid lines on the inner mandible).

front: What does the orbicularis oris do, and what is unusual about its origin?
back: Closes the lips; it has no real bony origin — it is rimmed by insertions of other facial muscles.

front: Which muscle forms the innermost muscle wall of the cheek?
back: The buccinator.

front: Primary functions of the buccinator?
back: Pulls the mouth corners laterally and holds food between the teeth while chewing.

front: What is the maxillary tuberosity?
back: The most distal (posterior) portion of the maxillary alveolar ridge.

front: What is the hamular (pterygomaxillary) notch used for?
back: A deep depression behind the tuberosity; a guide to the posterior border of a maxillary denture.

front: Hard vs soft palate: what proportion of the palatal vault is each?
back: Hard: anterior two-thirds (bone-supported). Soft: posterior one-third (muscular, mobile).

front: What does the incisive papilla cover?
back: The incisive foramen, in the midline just behind the central incisors.

front: Where are the rugae found?
back: Irregular fibrous ridges in the anterior one-third of the hard palate.

front: What is the vibrating line?
back: The line of flexion between the hard and soft palates, usually between the hamular notches near the foveae.

front: What forms the palatine foveae?
back: Groupings of minor palatine salivary glands (two depressions beside the midline near the vibrating line).

front: Name two reasons the retromolar pads matter in denture work.
back: They guide the plane of occlusion (position stays constant after extraction) and give distal support to a mandibular denture.

front: Where is the mental foramen normally located?
back: Buccal surface, between and slightly below the root tips of the first and second premolars.

front: What is the glenoid fossa?
back: A deep hollow on the undersurface of the zygomatic process of the temporal bone, housing the condyle in hinge movement.

front: What does the condyle do during protrusive movement?
back: Both condyles leave the fossae and move onto the articular eminences.

front: What is the articular disc made of, and what is its role?
back: Tough flexible fibrocartilage between condyle and fossa; a shock absorber that travels with the condyle.

front: How many anterior and posterior teeth are in one permanent arch?
back: Six anteriors (canine to canine) and ten posteriors.

front: What tissue forms the bulk of a tooth?
back: Dentin.

front: Through what opening do nerves and vessels enter the tooth?
back: The apical foramen, at or near the root apex.

front: What is the lamina dura?
back: A thin, dense layer of bone lining the tooth socket — a continuation of the cortical plate.

front: What suspends a tooth in its socket?
back: The periodontal ligament.

front: Which tissue is part of both the tooth and the periodontium?
back: Cementum.

front: Free vs attached gingiva?
back: Free gingiva can be displaced (crest to sulcus bottom); attached gingiva is firmly fixed to underlying bone.

front: In the Universal system, which tooth is #1 and which is #17?
back: #1 = upper right third molar; #17 = lower left third molar.

front: Universal numbers 1–16 vs 17–32?
back: 1–16 maxillary arch; 17–32 mandibular arch.

front: Which plane divides the body into right and left parts?
back: The sagittal plane.

front: Which plane divides the body into anterior and posterior parts?
back: The frontal plane.

front: Which plane divides the body into upper and lower parts?
back: The transverse (horizontal) plane.

front: Medial and lateral are synonyms for what?
back: Medial = internal; lateral = external (relative to the midsagittal plane).

front: Mesial vs distal surface?
back: Mesial: proximal surface closest to the arch midline. Distal: proximal surface away from it.

front: Incisal vs occlusal?
back: Incisal: cutting edge of an anterior tooth. Occlusal: chewing surface of a posterior tooth.

front: What is a line angle, and how many per tooth?
back: The junction of two crown surfaces; eight per tooth.

front: What is a point angle, and how many per tooth?
back: The junction of three crown surfaces; four per tooth.

front: What is an embrasure?
back: A space diverging from the contacting proximal surfaces of two adjacent teeth.

front: What is 'gauge' a measure of?
back: Thickness — e.g., wire/wire-wax diameter or sheet wax/metal thickness.

front: Define centric occlusion.
back: The occlusion of teeth when the mandible is in centric relation; may or may not coincide with MI.

front: In MI, how far forward of centric relation are most people's condyles?
back: About 1.25 mm ± 1 mm.

front: Vertical vs horizontal overlap?
back: Vertical: maxillary teeth extend over mandibular vertically in MI. Horizontal: projection beyond antagonists horizontally.

front: Angle Class II: where is the MB cusp of the upper first molar?
back: Anterior to the buccal groove of the lower first molar (retrognathic profile).

front: Angle Class III: molar relationship and profile?
back: Upper first molar MB cusp falls posterior to the lower buccal groove; prognathic profile.

front: Which cusps are stamp cusps?
back: Lingual cusps of the upper and buccal cusps of the lower.

front: Typical difference between occlusal vertical dimension and physiologic rest?
back: OVD is 2–4 mm less than the rest measurement.

front: What is Christensen's phenomenon?
back: The space between opposing occlusal surfaces during protrusion; anteriors disclude the posteriors.

front: In group function, what contacts on the nonworking side?
back: No contact between upper and lower teeth.

front: Mutually protected articulation: anterior overlaps in MI?
back: Horizontal 0.0–0.5 mm; vertical 2 mm or more.

front: What teeth contact on the working side in canine-guided articulation?
back: Only the upper and lower canines.

front: What are the three articulator categories by adjustability?
back: Nonadjustable, semiadjustable, fully adjustable.

front: What movements can a hinge-type articulator make?
back: Only opening and closing — no lateral or protrusive excursions.

front: Which articulator category is most used in the Dental Services, and for what?
back: Semiadjustable: all removable prostheses and moderately complex fixed work.

front: Where does the data for a fully adjustable articulator come from?
back: Mandibular movement tracings — pantographic or stereographic recordings.

front: What does 'arcon' stand for and describe?
back: ARticulator + CONdyle: condyle elements on the lower member, fossae on the upper, as in anatomy.

front: What does a facebow transfer do?
back: Mounts the maxillary cast relating it to the articulator condyles as the maxilla relates to the TMJs.

front: Effect of more water (higher W:P) on gypsum crushing strength?
back: Lowers strength — more porosity, fewer crystals per volume.

front: Effect of overmixing gypsum on strength?
back: Breaks forming crystals and reduces crushing strength (mixing up to ~1 min increases it).

front: Effect of more water on gypsum setting time?
back: Lengthens setting time.

front: Name two gypsum accelerators and three retarders.
back: Accelerators: potassium sulfate, table salt. Retarders: vinegar, potassium citrate, borax.

front: Why never add chemical accelerators/retarders to casting or soldering investments?
back: They also reduce setting expansion and crushing strength.

front: What is slurry water used for?
back: Accelerating plaster/stone set, e.g. in cast mounting.

front: Thick mix and long mixing time — effect on setting expansion?
back: Both increase setting expansion.

front: Allowed setting expansion range for model plaster?
back: 0.2–0.3 percent (0.3% maximum).

front: How is dental stone manufactured vs plaster?
back: Gypsum is autoclaved under pressure (plaster is heated in open vats), giving more regular prismatic particles.

front: Typical initial and final set of dental stone?
back: Initial 8–15 minutes; final about 45 minutes.

front: Setting expansion of die (improved) stone?
back: 0.08–0.18 percent.

front: How are improved stones made?
back: Gypsum boiled in 30% calcium chloride solution before autoclaving.

front: What are investments composed of?
back: A refractory (cristobalite or quartz) plus a binder (gypsum, phosphate or silicate).

front: Cristobalite vs quartz investments — which expands more?
back: Cristobalite.

front: About how much does gold alloy shrink on solidifying?
back: About 1.4% (±0.2%) — the mold must be enlarged to compensate.

front: Why can't a soldering investment be used for casting?
back: Its quartz refractory gives minimal expansion — not enough to offset gold shrinkage.

front: High-heat chrome-alloy investment: components?
back: Quartz powder with ethyl silicate liquid (for 2700–2800 °F chrome alloys).

front: Powder into water or water into powder for gypsum?
back: Always add powder to water.

front: How long to hold a phosphate-bonded investment under vacuum, and why?
back: 30 seconds — it releases ammonia gas; vacuum removes gas and air.

front: Should you add powder or water to a gypsum mix in progress?
back: Never — start a new mix; adding weakens and distorts.

front: When must a batch of investment be discarded for slow set?
back: If initial set takes more than 20 minutes.

front: Three groups of dental waxes?
back: Impression, pattern, processing.

front: Main components of baseplate wax?
back: Beeswax, paraffin, coloring.

front: Hard vs medium baseplate wax — when used?
back: Hard for warmer climates (resists flow); medium for cooler conditions.

front: Inlay wax Type B vs Type C?
back: Type B: direct (intraoral) technique. Type C: indirect (laboratory) technique.

front: Role of carnauba in inlay wax?
back: Controls the softening point and hardness.

front: Key property of sticky wax?
back: Breaks under pressure instead of bending — natural resin gives adhesiveness/hardness.

front: Main laboratory use of utility wax?
back: Beading impressions before pouring the cast.

front: What is boxing wax used for?
back: Boxing impressions; strips about 1½ × 12 in.

front: What is undercut (blockout) wax made of?
back: Beeswax, resin and kaolin.

front: What is disclosing wax used for?
back: Detecting points of unequal pressure when seating castings.

front: Temperature for a beeswax dip to seal refractory casts?
back: 280–300 °F (cast heated and dehydrated first).

front: Heat-cured denture resin: powder and liquid are?
back: Powder = polymer; liquid = monomer (with inhibitor; flammable, irritant).

front: Why are self-curing resins preferred for denture repair?
back: The denture need not undergo high curing temperature.

front: Which soft liners are the most truly elastic?
back: Silicone resin liners.

front: How does the ADA classify alloys?
back: By percentage of noble metals.

front: Name the noble metals.
back: Gold and the platinum group: platinum, palladium, ruthenium, rhodium, osmium, iridium.

front: Why do silver-containing metal-ceramic alloys risk problems?
back: Silver can green the porcelain and contaminate the furnace muffle.

front: What casting problem rises with palladium content?
back: Hydrogen gas absorption, making casting harder.

front: ADA minimum for chromium+cobalt+nickel in cast chrome alloys?
back: At least 85% by weight.

front: Specific gravity of chrome alloys vs gold?
back: About half — lighter castings.

front: Role of fluxes (K, Na, Ca oxides) in porcelain?
back: Lower the softening temperature and increase thermal expansion.

front: Most common intermediate oxide in porcelain and its effect?
back: Aluminum oxide — increases hardness and viscosity.

front: Common porcelain opacifiers?
back: Cerium, titanium and zirconium oxides.

front: Tinfoil thickness for the stone cast vs the waxed denture?
back: 0.001 in on the cast; 0.003 in over the waxed denture.

front: What are tinfoil substitutes made of?
back: Sodium or potassium alginate in distilled water.

front: Which flux form is best for casting?
back: Powdered flux.

front: Give a common antiflux.
back: Pencil lead (graphite).

front: Why isn't isopropyl alcohol recommended for the torch?
back: It smokes badly when applied to wax.

front: Sulfuric acid's advantage over hydrochloric as a pickle?
back: No objectionable fumes.

front: Composition of aqua regia?
back: 3 parts hydrochloric acid : 1 part nitric acid; dissolves gold and platinum.

front: Hydrofluoric acid: lab use and first-aid item to keep nearby?
back: Dissolving porcelain off metal; magnesium oxide ointment.

front: Which polishing agent is not recommended for acrylic, and why?
back: Rouge — collects in crevices around denture teeth.

front: What is Carborundum?
back: Silicon carbide.

front: Hardest abrasive known?
back: Diamond.

front: Typical melting range of chrome alloys, and a suitable flame?
back: Over 2600 °F; oxyacetylene.

front: How is impression compound softened and hardened?
back: Softened by heat; hardened by cooling.

front: Need a separator when pouring gypsum into compound?
back: No.

front: How should a low-fusing wax impression be rinsed?
back: Carefully with room-temperature water, without touching the tissue side.

front: Principal ingredients of impression paste?
back: Zinc oxide and eugenol (or lauric acid).

front: Most accurate elastomeric impression materials?
back: Polyethers and polysiloxanes.

front: Why pour condensation silicones promptly?
back: Shrinkage occurs after about 30 minutes.

front: Pour polysulfide and condensation silicone impressions within?
back: 25 minutes.

front: Why can't polyether impressions be die-plated?
back: Highly hydrophilic; water sorption changes dimensions.

front: Agar vs alginate hydrocolloid?
back: Agar is reversible; alginate is irreversible.

front: What happens to gelled hydrocolloid exposed to water or air?
back: It changes dimensions.

front: Effect of hydrocolloid exudate on gypsum?
back: Makes the gypsum surface soft and chalky.

front: How are alginate impressions disinfected?
back: Spray, then sealed plastic bag — not immersed.

front: Pour alginate impressions within how long?
back: 12 minutes.

front: Which disinfectant should addition silicone/polysulfide NOT be immersed in?
back: Neutral glutaraldehyde.

front: How are polyether impressions disinfected?
back: Like hydrocolloids — spray, not immersion; chlorine-based, short time.

front: How can a contaminated stone cast be disinfected?
back: 0.5% sodium hypochlorite in clear SDS, 30-minute soak.

front: From what is slurry dihydrate solution prepared?
back: Freshly set stone never poured against a contaminated impression.

front: Maximum compressed air pressure for cleaning?
back: 30 lb/in².

front: Recommended Bunsen burner flame height?
back: About 3 inches.

front: Rule for eye protection?
back: Wear glasses/goggles whenever any possibility of eye damage exists.

front: Sharp vs dull instruments — which is more dangerous?
back: Dull.

front: Rule about running lathes?
back: Never leave unattended; turn off when not in use.

front: Where to use acids with toxic fumes?
back: Under a power exhaust hood.

front: Hepatitis B risk for lab technicians?
back: Almost three times the general population.

front: Key infection control concept in the lab?
back: Clean and disinfect contaminated items before reaching the production area.

front: What is the receiving area?
back: A separate engineering control for disinfecting incoming items.

front: PPE in the receiving area?
back: Gloves, mask, eye protection, smocks.

front: Disinfecting incoming prostheses?
back: Rinse/scrub, ultrasonic cleaner, then tuberculocidal disinfectant.

front: How is a finished prosthesis returned?
back: Cleaned, disinfected, bagged.

front: Universal precautions mean?
back: Treat all human blood and OPIM as infectious.

source.ref: OSHA Fact Sheet: Bloodborne Pathogens Standard (29 CFR 1910.1030)

front: Hepatitis B vaccine: when must it be offered?
back: After BBP training, within 10 days of initial assignment to a job with occupational exposure.

source.ref: OSHA Fact Sheet: Bloodborne Pathogens Standard (29 CFR 1910.1030)

front: Define exposure incident.
back: Eye, mouth, mucous membrane, non-intact skin or parenteral contact with blood/OPIM.

source.ref: OSHA Fact Sheet: Bloodborne Pathogens Standard (29 CFR 1910.1030)

front: How often is BBP training?
back: At assignment, annually, and when tasks change.

source.ref: OSHA Fact Sheet: Bloodborne Pathogens Standard (29 CFR 1910.1030)

front: How many SDS sections, and which is first-aid?
back: 16; Section 4.

source.ref: OSHA Brief: Hazard Communication Standard Safety Data Sheets (OSHA 3514)

front: Which SDS section covers PPE?
back: Section 8.

source.ref: OSHA Brief: Hazard Communication Standard Safety Data Sheets (OSHA 3514)

front: HazCom pictogram format?
back: A symbol on a white background framed by a red border.

source.ref: OSHA QuickCard: Hazard Communication Standard Pictogram (OSHA 3491)

front: Pictogram for skin corrosion or corrosive to metals?
back: Corrosion.

source.ref: OSHA QuickCard: Hazard Communication Standard Pictogram (OSHA 3491)

front: Pictogram for gases under pressure?
back: Gas cylinder.

source.ref: OSHA QuickCard: Hazard Communication Standard Pictogram (OSHA 3491)
